title: Typing | Fun Facts: People and Progress
description: This course is for the continued development of typing skills for students who have already mastered touch typing basics using one of our instructional typing courses, such as Typing Jungle. Students will type and discover fun facts relating to people, progress, culture, architecture, inventors and more in 200 lessons.

lessons.name: U.S. History Introduction
lessons.text1: The United States has an eventful history for such a young nation. Try typing through these surprising facts to learn more about the U.S.

lessons.name: Harvard University
lessons.text1: Harvard University is the oldest university in America, founded in 1636.

lessons.name: Liberty Bell
lessons.text1: The Liberty Bell, a symbol of American independence, was actually forged in England!

lessons.name: Texas
lessons.text1: Texas was once its own independent country! The Republic of Texas existed from 1836 to 1845. Its president was Sam Houston.

lessons.name: St. Augustine
lessons.text1: The oldest city in the United States is none other than St. Augustine in Florida. Jamestown, Virginia is America's oldest English settlement.

lessons.name: Harriet Tubman
lessons.text1: Did you know that Harriet Tubman was a war hero? During the Civil War, she helped free 70 enslaved people in the Combahee River Raid.

lessons.name: Abraham Lincoln
lessons.text1: Abraham Lincoln was a wrestler! He may have participated in as many as 300 matches during his lifetime. Legend says that he only lost once.

lessons.name: Treats
lessons.text1: Two iconic treats come from the United States. In 1908, lollipops were invented by George Smith in New Haven, Connecticut. S'mores were invented in 1927 by a Girl Scout troop leader!

lessons.name: Mayflower
lessons.text1: How many descendants of the Mayflower exist today? 10 million Americans are estimated to be related to those who traveled across the Atlantic to Plymouth, and 35 million descendants exist worldwide.

lessons.name: Cheerleading
lessons.text1: Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Ronald Reagan, and George W. Bush were all cheerleaders in college. Cheerleading has been around since the late 1800s, and it was an all-male sport until the 1920s!

lessons.name: George Washington
lessons.text1: Lots of myths exist about America's first president, George Washington. While Washington did have dentures, they were not made of wood. The story about him cutting down a cherry tree as a boy was made up by a biographer.

lessons.name: Hollywood
lessons.text1: Hollywood is iconic when it comes to the film industry. The first Hollywood film was made over 100 years ago! The Count of Monte Cristo premiered in 1908 and was filmed partially in Hollywood and partially in Chicago.

lessons.name: Iroquois Confederacy
lessons.text1: The U.S. Constitution isn't as original as you might think! The Iroquois Confederacy was a league of six Indigenous nations. They collaborated on the Confederacy's Great Law of Peace, which allowed the nations to govern together.

lessons.name: White House
lessons.text1: The White House wasn't always known as the White House. Up until 1901, Americans called the building the President's Palace or House. Executive Mansion was also used. President Theodore Roosevelt was the one who named it the White House.

lessons.name: Jobs
lessons.text1: All presidents had jobs before taking office! Some had surprisingly interesting jobs before their political careers took off. Jimmy Carter, for example, was a peanut farmer. Harry Truman was a haberdasher, or a hat salesman. Ronald Reagan was a movie star!

lessons.name: War of 1812
lessons.text1: During the War of 1812, Washington, D.C. was attacked and occupied by British forces. As a result, much of Washington, D.C., including what is known today as the White House, burned. It took three years to make the mansion habitable once more. Today, you can still see some scorch marks on the exterior walls.

lessons.name: Sybil Ludington
lessons.text1: Paul Revere became famous for warning revolutionary Americans of an impending British attack during his midnight ride. But a teenage girl by the name of Sybil Ludington is alleged to have ridden even further on horseback in the driving rain. She rode forty miles to warn against an impending attack on Danbury, Connecticut.

lessons.name: American Flag
lessons.text1: A 17-year-old boy is responsible for the flag America flies today. In 1958, America was on the cusp of adding both Alaska and Hawaii to the list of states. Robert Heft drafted a new design with two additional stars for a high school project. Heft's design was submitted to the White House, and President Eisenhower selected it.

lessons.name: Ancient Civilizations Introduction
lessons.text1: Discover fun facts about ancient civilizations while improving your typing skills! Join us on a journey through history as you practice typing.

lessons.name: Agriculture
lessons.text1: About 12,000 years ago, in the Middle East and Asia, people decided roaming around wasn't the best way to live anymore. They planted crops and started living in one place by creating villages.

lessons.name: Sumer
lessons.text1: Around 5,000 years ago, in the region we now call southeastern Iraq, the ancient land of Sumer took center stage by launching civilization's very first empire.

lessons.name: Norte Chico
lessons.text1: The earliest known civilization in the Americas was called Norte Chico. It was located in what is now Peru. It declined and was eventually conquered by Europeans.

lessons.name: Greek Thought
lessons.text1: From 800 to 146 BCE, Greek thinkers laid the foundations for science, government, art, and math. Their big ideas shaped Western civilization and paved the way for Roman rule.

lessons.name: African Civilizations
lessons.text1: Ancient African civilizations like Carthage, Numidia, Punt, Nok, and D'mt were trailblazers in math, science, and art. Their legacies are amazing but are often overshadowed by European colonization.

lessons.name: Nile
lessons.text1: Ancient Egypt was the rock star of ancient civilizations! People living along the Nile's lush floodplains used the river to fuel their agriculture and their grand ambitions. Think colossal pyramids that still leave us scratching our heads.

lessons.name: Romans
lessons.text1: The Roman Republic lasted for about 500 years before becoming an empire. Rome massively shaped Western civilization in terms of religion, law, architecture, warfare, language, and more! At one point, Rome ruled the land from the Mediterranean to Iraq.

lessons.name: Persian Empire
lessons.text1: Founded by Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BCE, the breadth of the Persian Empire spanned from Turkey to Yemen. Despite it having three distinct dynasties (Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian), the overall impact of the Persian Empire was enormous!

lessons.name: Sword of Goujian
lessons.text1: Get ready for a legendary find! The ancient Sword of Goujian, buried for over 2,000 years, was unearthed in 1965 in China. It's still razor sharp!

lessons.name: Stonehenge
lessons.text1: Ancient movers alert! Between 2600 and 1600 BCE, the mysterious Bell Beaker civilization hauled 4-ton bluestones 150 miles to build Stonehenge, possibly for healing powers!

lessons.name: Nazca Lines
lessons.text1: Get ready for a mysterious adventure! Peru's giant 2,000-year-old Nazca Lines are only visible from the sky. The full meaning of these lines eludes researchers today. Drones found even more lines in 2018!

lessons.name: Trousers
lessons.text1: Central Asian horse-riders crafted the first pants between 1300 and 1000 BCE. Archeologists found these primitive pants in China. These ancient wool trousers featured straight legs, roomy fits, and waist strings. Talk about pioneering fashion for nomadic adventures!

lessons.name: Trajan's Market
lessons.text1: Did you know that the Romans built the world's first shopping mall? The Trajan's Market was built in Rome around 100 CE. It was designed by an architect named Apollodorus of Damascus, and it was filled with shops, offices, and apartments. It even had an elevator and a central heating system!

lessons.name: Cacao Beans
lessons.text1: Do you have a sweet tooth? As early as 600 BCE, the Maya people in Belize discovered cacao beans and whipped up a deliciously foamy drink with water, honey, chili peppers, and cornmeal. While other groups might have tasted the bean first, the Maya turned chocolate into a tasty, spicy adventure!

lessons.name: Ancient Noodles
lessons.text1: In 2005, archaeologists discovered 4,000-year-old noodles in northwestern China! The noodles were made from millet, which is a grain indigenous to China. These noodles were incredibly well-preserved and stored in an overturned bowl buried under 10 feet of sediment at the Lajia archaeological site.

lessons.name: Dogs
lessons.text1: Dog owners in the medieval era gave their pets adorable and affectionate names, just like today. Popular dog names included Jakke, Bo, Amiable, Clenche, Bragge, Nameles, Venus, Fortuna, Terri, Nosewise, and Whitefoot. Some blacksmiths called their dogs Hemmerli, which means "little hammer." So cute!

lessons.name: Ancient Honey
lessons.text1: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that are still edible after thousands of years. Honey's unique chemical composition is the secret to its resilience; most bacteria and microorganisms cannot survive in it. As long as honey is well-sealed in a jar, it'll stay safe to eat for a long time!

lessons.name: Music Introduction
lessons.text1: Whether you realize it or not, music is all around us! Practice your typing skills while discovering interesting facts about music.

lessons.name: Group Singing
lessons.text1: Group singing has physical and emotional benefits, releasing feel-good hormones and reducing stress levels.

lessons.name: Exercise
lessons.text1: Studies show that syncing music with repetitive exercise boosts performance, helping people train longer and more efficiently.

lessons.name: Space Songs
lessons.text1: In 2015, astronaut Chris Hadfield released Space Sessions: Songs for a Tin Can, an album of 11 songs entirely recorded during his 144 days in orbit.

lessons.name: Oldest Instrument
lessons.text1: The oldest musical instrument is a 50,000-year-old Neanderthal flute made from bear bones. This instrument was found in Slovenia and predates Homo sapiens.

lessons.name: Mozart
lessons.text1: In 2016, a 200-disc CD box set of Mozart's music was released for the 225th anniversary of his death. Sales from this artist's work surpassed sales from Beyonce, Adele, or Drake albums!

lessons.name: Metal Bands
lessons.text1: Finland has the most heavy metal bands per capita, with 53.5 per 100,000 people. While heavy metal originated in the U.S. and U.K., their per capita numbers are much lower, at 5.5 and 5.2, respectively.

lessons.name: Plant Music
lessons.text1: Certain frequencies from sound and music can boost key photosynthesis genes that help plants grow. Classical music can even promote seed germination. Playing music in a garden might not sound so strange!

lessons.name: The Beatles
lessons.text1: Did you know that one of the most iconic bands of all time couldn't read or write sheet music? The Beatles relied on ear training, meaning they hummed tunes, memorized melodies, and recreated them. Formal music training may not always be essential for success.

lessons.name: Bessie Smith
lessons.text1: Bessie Smith was known as the "Empress of the Blues." She was a 1920s blues singer and icon whose dramatic style influenced many other artists.

lessons.name: Aerosmith
lessons.text1: Aerosmith and Run-DMC's 1986 hit "Walk This Way" is seen as the first mainstream rock-rap crossover, earning both groups spots in the Rock Hall of Fame.

lessons.name: Beethoven
lessons.text1: Despite near-total deafness by age 44, Beethoven composed iconic pieces like Symphony No. 5 and No. 9, relying on memory and "inner ears" to craft his works.

lessons.name: Orchestra
lessons.text1: Did you know that an orchestra can vary in size? Chamber orchestras have up to 50 performers, while symphony and philharmonic orchestras often have over 80 people.

lessons.name: Oldest Composition
lessons.text1: The world's oldest musical composition dates back to the 1st century CE. The Seikilos Epitaph was found in 1883 on a Turkish grave marker, its lyrics urging people to "shine."

lessons.name: Fender
lessons.text1: The founder of the iconic electric guitar brand Fender never learned to play the guitar. Despite this, Leo Fender was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1992.

lessons.name: Animal Beats
lessons.text1: Have you ever met an animal who can keep time with a beat? Turns out, sea lions have rhythm! A sea lion named Ronan was the first non-human mammal to show that she can move to a beat by bobbing her head along to the groovy music of Earth, Wind, and Fire and the Backstreet Boys.

lessons.name: Catchiest Song
lessons.text1: Researchers at England's Museum of Science and Industry conducted a study to find the catchiest song of all time. They tested 12,000 people on 1,000 pop song snippets from the 1940s onward, and "Wannabe" by the Spice Girls was the fastest recognized song. Listeners could identify it in just 2.3 seconds!

lessons.name: John Cage
lessons.text1: The world's slowest and longest musical performance has been playing on an organ since 2001 in Germany. Set to last 639 years, this performance won't be finished until 2640! John Cage, the composer for this musical experiment, died in 1992 but left instructions for the organ to be played "as slow as possible."

lessons.name: Scientific Discoveries Introduction
lessons.text1: People have found some amazing ways to advance society. Enhance your typing skills while exploring groundbreaking scientific discoveries!

lessons.name: Penicillin
lessons.text1: Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, marked the start of antibiotics and revolutionized treatment for infections.

lessons.name: Xenobots
lessons.text1: Scientists have created "xenobots," or tiny living robots made from frog cells. These small cells can swim, self-repair, and move particles in their environment.

lessons.name: Cow Restrooms
lessons.text1: Scientists have successfully trained cows to use designated bathroom stalls, collecting their urine to reduce environmental pollution and possibly use it as fertilizer in the future.

lessons.name: Velcro
lessons.text1: In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral observed burdock burrs clinging to his clothes and dog's fur after a hike. He was inspired to invent the fastening system we now know as Velcro.

lessons.name: Black Holes
lessons.text1: In 2019, astronomers captured the first image of a supermassive black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy. This helps scientists better understand the behavior of such massive entities believed to reside at the centers of most galaxies.

lessons.name: Pacemaker
lessons.text1: In 1956, Wilson Greatbatch accidentally used an incorrect resistor while building a heart rhythm recorder. This led to the invention of a small device known as the pacemaker. This device was first successfully implanted in a dog before tried on humans.

lessons.name: Play-Doh
lessons.text1: In the 1930s, Noah McVicker developed a non-toxic, putty-like substance as a wallpaper cleaner to remove soot from walls. By the 1950s, with the advent of washable vinyl wallpaper, McVicker's nephew, Joseph McVicker, rebranded the product as "Play-Doh."

lessons.name: Shortest Day
lessons.text1: Have you ever wondered what the shortest day on record was? Very few days are exactly 24 hours. The speed of the Earth's rotation is affected by factors such as seasons and climate. As of 2023, the shortest day on record, June 29, 2022, was nearly 1.6 milliseconds under 24 hours!

lessons.name: Magnets
lessons.text1: Did you know that temperature impacts the magnetism of magnets? Heating up magnets causes them to lose their magnetic strength. Cooling them down makes them more magnetic.

lessons.name: Problem-Solving Birds
lessons.text1: A study from Erich Jarvis' lab found that animals capable of complex vocal learning, like starlings and blue jays, also excel in problem-solving tasks. This suggests a link between vocal learning and intelligence.

lessons.name: Corn Flakes
lessons.text1: In 1894, John and Will Kellogg accidentally overcooked wheat. When rolled out, it formed flakes, which they baked into a crispy snack. Experimenting with corn yielded similar results, leading to the creation of Corn Flakes.

lessons.name: Solar Panels
lessons.text1: As an undergraduate, Nate Cira observed food coloring droplets moving as if alive. At Stanford, he and Manu Prakash discovered that surface tension and evaporation caused this behavior, leading to potential applications like self-cleaning solar panels.

lessons.name: Wasps
lessons.text1: Did you know wasps can socialize? While studying wasps, Liz Tibbetts discovered they have unique facial markings and can recognize each other. Her research showed that wasps evolved to distinguish individuals, allowing for social interactions within their wasp colonies.

lessons.name: Lungs
lessons.text1: Researchers Ali Brivanlou and Charles M. Rice have developed a platform that uses microchips to grow genetically identical "micro lungs" from human embryonic stem cells. These replicate the complexity of lung tissue, helping researchers analyze lung infections and diseases.

lessons.name: Mummy
lessons.text1: Researchers have recreated the voice of Nesyamun, a 3,000-year-old Egyptian mummy. They reconstructed his vocal tract using medical imaging, 3D printing, and an electronic larynx. Researchers used these items to produce a single vowel sound thought to sound like the mummy's voice.

lessons.name: Copper
lessons.text1: Doorknobs are known as high-touch surfaces because people frequently touch them. But did you know some doorknobs can clean themselves? Many brass and copper doorknobs can disinfect themselves within 8 hours as a result of the oligodynamic effect. Bacteria can't survive long on brass and copper!

lessons.name: Super Glue
lessons.text1: In 1942, Dr. Harry Coover was researching weapon-making materials for World War II when he found a substance too sticky for this purpose and set it aside. Then, in 1951, he accidentally stuck two lenses together with the same substance and couldn't get them apart. He went on to develop and market the substance as "Super Glue."

lessons.name: Innovative Inventions Introduction
lessons.text1: Over the years, humans have come up with some innovative inventions. Let's practice your typing skills while we learn about some of the more unusual inventions in the world!
The Eiffel Tower was inaugurated in Paris the same year that Nintendo was founded in Kyoto. Both happened in 1889. Nintendo was a playing card company before video games were invented.

lessons.name: Breakfast Cereal
lessons.text1: The first breakfast cereal had to be soaked in milk overnight. It was manufactured in 1863 using graham flour that was baked twice to a very hard texture. Cereal wasn't a popular breakfast option when it first came out.

lessons.name: Tennis for Two
lessons.text1: The first computer game created solely for entertainment purposes was called "Tennis for Two." It was designed in 1958 by William Higinbotham, an American physicist. The gameplay involves two players hitting a digital tennis ball back and forth across a court.

lessons.name: Cloud Sculptures
lessons.text1: Make your own cloud! A Dutch artist named Berndnaut Smilde makes clouds out of smoke and water vapor. They are created in cold spaces with no air circulation. His clouds only last about 10 seconds, but he works with photographers. He calls his clouds "temporary sculptures"!

lessons.name: Mobile Phones
lessons.text1: Can you guess when the first mobile phone was invented? It was invented in 1973! It was called the DynaTAC 8000x, weighed about 2 pounds, took 10 hours to charge, and had a battery life of about 30 minutes. It cost $3,995 at the time, which is equivalent to over $10,000 today.

lessons.name: Trivial Pursuit
lessons.text1: Have you ever played the game Trivial Pursuit? It was invented in Montreal, Quebec in 1979 by Chris Haney and Scott Abbott. They were unable to find some of the pieces from their Scrabble game, so they decided to invent a new game instead. They came up with Trivial Pursuit in just a few hours!

lessons.name: Mystery Flavor
lessons.text1: Have you ever tasted a Dum-Dums lollipop with a white wrapper and wondered what flavor it is? These "mystery flavor" lollipops are actually created by blending the last bit of flavor from one batch with the first bit from the next, rather than stopping and cleaning out the machine between batches!

lessons.name: Theremin
lessons.text1: In 1919, a Russian physicist named Leon Theremin invented a musical instrument that you can play without any physical contact at all! You play the theremin by waving your hands between two metal antennas. One of the most famous classical thereminists is Clara Rockmore, who was formerly a violinist.

lessons.name: Stilts
lessons.text1: You might be used to seeing stilts in parades or at the circus, but they were actually invented for a completely different purpose: sheep herding! In 6th century France, sheep herders used stilts to navigate wet marshy areas with greater ease. These wooden stilts were called tchangues, or "Big Legs."

lessons.name: Webcam
lessons.text1: Did you know that the first webcam was used to monitor a coffee pot? Back in 1991, researchers at the University of Cambridge set up a camera pointed at their office coffee maker so that they could see whether the pot was full or empty from their computers! It was called the "Trojan Room coffee pot."

lessons.name: Stalactites
lessons.text1: The Great Stalacpipe Organ is one of the largest instruments! It's located in Luray Caverns and took three years to create. You play it by pressing keys on an organ. Each key corresponds to rubber mallets that tap against 37 different stalactites in the cavern, which are each tuned to a specific tone.

lessons.name: Mars Men
lessons.text1: Sour Patch Kids were originally called "Mars Men" when they were first created in the 1970s. These deliciously sour candies were inspired by space aliens and the public's interest in all things space-related! They were changed to Sour Patch Kids in the 1980s, inspired by children's love of Cabbage Patch Kids.

lessons.name: Speedcubing
lessons.text1: Have you ever solved a Rubik's Cube? There are championships for "speedcubing" all over the world. But did you know this popular puzzle was actually invented by accident? The inventor, Erno Rubik, was experimenting with interlocking mechanisms, and he didn't know he'd created a puzzle until it was all scrambled!

lessons.name: Goofybike
lessons.text1: In 1939, Charles Steinlauf introduced an unusual family bicycle. He sat on the very top of the bike and steered it with a large steering wheel. His son pedaled from the back, his daughter sat on the handlebars in the front, and his wife operated a sewing machine in the middle. It was rightfully named the Goofybike!

lessons.name: Microwave
lessons.text1: Did you know that the microwave oven was basically invented by accident? A physicist named Percy Spencer was working on magnetrons when he noticed that the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He realized the microwaves from the radar had caused the chocolate to melt! Spencer went on to patent the first microwave oven in 1945.

lessons.name: Computer Mouse
lessons.text1: In 1964, engineer Douglas Engelbart built the first prototype of a computer mouse. It was made of wood and had only one button! The cord extending from the back resembled a tail, which is how the mouse earned its name. The mouse was part of a larger project to develop new technologies that would enhance human-computer interaction.

lessons.name: Slinky
lessons.text1: Have you ever played with a Slinky? This popular toy was invented by accident in 1943 by Richard T. James, a naval engineer who was working on a way to stabilize sensitive equipment on ships during rough seas. When he accidentally knocked over a spring, he watched in amazement as it "walked" down a stack of books and onto the floor!

lessons.name: Culture Introduction
lessons.text1: Dive into learning about various cultures and gain tidbits on traditions, foods, art, and history while sharpening your typing skills.

lessons.name: Coffee
lessons.text1: Did you know there's an order to coffee drinking in Italy? Mornings are for cappuccinos, while espresso rules the rest of the day.

lessons.name: Fireworks
lessons.text1: Australia once had big fireworks displays on the Queen's Birthday and Empire Day, but this faded in the 1980s after many areas banned selling fireworks.

lessons.name: Currency
lessons.text1: On the South Atlantic island of Tristan da Cunha, potatoes were once used as currency. In Aztec and Maya cultures in Mesoamerica, cacao beans were also used as currency.

lessons.name: Mona Lisa
lessons.text1: The Mona Lisa gets love letters and even has her own mailbox at the Louvre in France! People are so captivated by her mysterious smile and eyes that fans from around the world write to her portrait.

lessons.name: Rolling Cheese
lessons.text1: Every spring in the U.K., people race down Cooper's Hill chasing a rolling cheese! The first to catch the 70 mph, 9-pound cheese wins it as a prize. This fun tradition has been around for over 200 years!

lessons.name: Olympic Arts
lessons.text1: Baron Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics, believed true Olympians excelled in art and sports. From 1912 to 1948, medals were awarded for sports-inspired works in art, literature, and music!

lessons.name: Noodles
lessons.text1: In Chinese culture, longevity noodles symbolize a wish for a long life and are staples at celebrations. Eating uncut noodles reflects health and prosperity while sharing them highlights family and life milestones.

lessons.name: Magpies
lessons.text1: Traditions about luck tend to come from superstitions. For example, while some Native American tribes view magpies as brave birds, many people in England consider them bad luck. In fact, to ward this bird off, the English sometimes salute or say "good morning" to magpies!

lessons.name: Baby Teeth
lessons.text1: In Greece, kids toss baby teeth on the roof of their homes for good luck and to welcome a healthy adult tooth. No tooth fairy here!

lessons.name: Tightrope
lessons.text1: In the small, remote village of Tsovkra-1 in southern Russia, every resident without a disability can walk a tightrope. It is a skill taught to children in school.

lessons.name: Papua New Guinea
lessons.text1: More than 850 languages are spoken in Papua New Guinea, a country with just 7.6 million people. Many of them are only understood by a few thousand people or fewer.

lessons.name: Ethiopian Food
lessons.text1: Ethiopian food is all about fun and sharing! Instead of forks, you use your hands and tear pieces of injera, a spongy flatbread, to scoop up tasty stews. It's like using edible utensils!

lessons.name: Flamenco
lessons.text1: Flamenco from Spain is an iconic mix of music and dance! Bright costumes, passionate moves, and powerful rhythms make it unforgettable. Like mariachi in Mexico, flamenco shows how music connects us all!

lessons.name: New Year's Eve
lessons.text1: In Bolivia, it's a New Year's Eve tradition to bake money into cakes and pastries! If you find a coin in your slice, it's said to bring good luck for the new year. Bakeries across the country join in on the fun!

lessons.name: La Tomatina
lessons.text1: Who doesn't love a food fight? Every year in Buñol, Spain, people gather for La Tomatina, the world's biggest tomato fight! Thousands join this messy, fun event, tossing tomatoes at each other from all around the globe.

lessons.name: Red
lessons.text1: Did you know brides in India often wear red on their wedding day? Red is a lucky color in many cultures! Hindu brides wear gorgeous saris or lehengas, depending on their region. It's a beautiful tradition celebrating love and good fortune!

lessons.name: Line Sitters
lessons.text1: Do you like standing in line? You might be able to do it professionally! Line standers, also known as "line sitters" or "queue standers," are paid to stand in line for their clients, sometimes for hours or days. Line standers are usually in line to buy a product or gain entry to important political hearings.

lessons.name: Daring Feats Introduction
lessons.text1: Do you enjoy a fun dare? The following facts are all about experiences that test limits. Let's practice your typing skills while you learn about some daring feats!

lessons.name: Free Solo
lessons.text1: Alex Honnold is an American big wall free solo climber famous for his climbs up several rock walls in Yosemite.

lessons.name: Plank
lessons.text1: George Hood set the Guinness World Record for the longest plank in 2011, holding the position for 1 hour, 20 minutes, and 5.01 seconds. He set this record at age 54!

lessons.name: Surfing
lessons.text1: Surfing champion Gary Saavedra set records in 2011 by surfing a wave in the Panama Canal for 3 hours, 55 minutes, and 2 seconds. His surfing distance covered 41.3 miles.

lessons.name: Niagara Falls
lessons.text1: Nik Wallenda is an American aerialist and acrobat known for high-wire performances without a safety net. In 2012, he became the first person to walk a tightrope directly over Niagara Falls.

lessons.name: Magician
lessons.text1: David Blaine is a magician who set and broke several world records. In his "Above the Below" stunt, he was sealed inside a transparent case and suspended above London's River Thames for 44 days without food.

lessons.name: Zazel
lessons.text1: Rosa Richter, known as "Zazel," became the first human cannonball at London's Royal Aquarium in 1877. She was launched high into the air by a spring-powered device then landed in a large net, astonishing spectators.

lessons.name: Helen Gibson
lessons.text1: Helen Gibson was a master of trick horse riding, performing her own stunts on horseback from an early age. This led her to become a stunt double in movies in the 1910s. In one film, she even leapt from a building onto a moving train!

lessons.name: Drag Racing
lessons.text1: Shirley Roque loved driving fast in a car and, in the late 1950s, she embraced the new, popular activity known as drag racing. Despite initial resistance from the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA), she achieved amateur victories and became the first woman to race in the "Top Gas" category in 1968.

lessons.name: Daring Feats Game 1
lessons.text1: climber Yosemite plank surfing tightrope magician cannonball horseback racing acrobat

lessons.name: Motocross
lessons.text1: Robbie "Maddo" Maddison pioneered motocross surfing by riding incredible waves in Tahiti on his motorcycle. He prepared for this feat for three years!

lessons.name: Ostrich Racing
lessons.text1: Ostrich racing is a unique sport where participants ride ostriches. Sounds easy, right? Well, watch out, because these birds can run up to 70 kilometers per hour, or roughly 43 miles per hour!

lessons.name: Wim Hof
lessons.text1: Wim Hof is a Dutch adventurer known for immersing himself in ice for 1 hour, 13 minutes, and 48 seconds, breaking his own previous Guinness World Record. This earned him the nickname "The Iceman."

lessons.name: Skyaking
lessons.text1: Invented by Miles Daisher, skyaking combines kayaking and parachuting to create an intense ride. A person jumps from an aircraft in a kayak and lands on the water after their exhilarating ride through the sky.

lessons.name: Zorbing
lessons.text1: Have you ever wanted to be a hamster? Then zorbing might be for you! First popularized in New Zealand, zorbing is also known as sphereing or globe-riding. This is an activity where a person gets inside a giant plastic orb and rolls along a gentle hill or level surface.

lessons.name: Kitty O'Neil
lessons.text1: Despite losing her hearing as an infant, Kitty O'Neil pursued her passion for speed, racing motorcycles, speedboats, and rocket-fueled cars. In the 1970s, she became a Hollywood stuntwoman, performing daring feats in films and TV shows like "The Bionic Woman" and "Wonder Woman."

lessons.name: Philippe Petit
lessons.text1: In 1974, a man named Philippe Petit illegally walked on a cable he rigged between the Twin Towers in New York City. He walked 400 meters above the ground! Previously, he illegally walked between the towers of the Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris in 1971 and the Sydney Harbor Bridge in Australia in 1973.

lessons.name: Extreme Ironing
lessons.text1: Do you like having neat, pressed clothes and doing extreme sports? Then extreme ironing might be for you! Participants of extreme ironing, or EI, bring an ironing board to an unusual location, like a mountaintop or the top of a statue, and then iron their clothes. Some even iron while snowboarding or canoeing!

lessons.name: Goanna Pulling
lessons.text1: Goanna Pulling is an Australian sport inspired by the native goanna species of lizard. Competitors take a lizard-like position and play tug-of-war by pulling another competitor using a strap around each person's neck. This feat is risky since participants often end up with injuries or burns to their necks from the straps.

lessons.name: Fascinating Figures Introduction
lessons.text1: History is full of fascinating figures who have done amazing things. Practice your typing skills while discovering interesting facts about these people!

lessons.name: Pablo Picasso
lessons.text1: Pablo Picasso is one of the world's most famous artists. He invented a style known as Cubism as well as the concept of the collage.

lessons.name: Cleopatra
lessons.text1: Cleopatra ruled Egypt for almost 30 years and managed to heighten Egypt's wealth and power at a time when men typically controlled society.

lessons.name: Ismail al-Jazari
lessons.text1: Ismail al-Jazari from Turkey created an inventive book of mechanics in 1206. It changed history and influenced technology and engineering for generations!

lessons.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
lessons.text1: French military and political leader Napoleon Bonaparte fought and lost many wars in the early 1800s, but his military systems and ideas were revolutionary.

lessons.name: Shakespeare
lessons.text1: William Shakespeare is thought to be one of the greatest writers of all time. He created around 38 plays that were based on history, politics, and even other authors' works.

lessons.name: Bessie Coleman
lessons.text1: In 1921, Bessie Coleman became the first African American woman and Native American woman to be issued a pilot's license. She earned her license in France because of racial discrimination in the United States.

lessons.name: Bruce Lee
lessons.text1: Bruce Lee fascinates many with his martial arts moves, appearing in over 13 films. His acting is known throughout the world, and he influenced the way Asian actors were portrayed in movies.

lessons.name: Cristiano Ronaldo
lessons.text1: Cristiano Ronaldo of Portugal is one of the world's best and most famous soccer players. He's received hundreds of trophies in his lifetime and is considered an inspiration to many in the world of soccer.

lessons.name: Fascinating Figures Game 1
lessons.text1: Picasso Cleopatra Egypt engineering Napoleon military pilot Coleman Shakespeare Ronaldo

lessons.name: Joan of Arc
lessons.text1: Joan of Arc became an important part of the Hundred Years' War when she led the French army to victory against the English. She did this at the age of seventeen!

lessons.name: Genghis Khan
lessons.text1: Genghis Khan built the Mongol Empire, one of the largest empires in history. He did so by creating a massive army and perfecting the accuracy of horse-mounted archers. His empire covered 12 million square miles.

lessons.name: Catherine of Aragon
lessons.text1: Catherine of Aragon was the first wife of Henry VIII. This Spanish-born queen of England was a devout Catholic. She was married to King Henry VIII for 24 years until their marriage was annulled and he married Anne Boleyn.

lessons.name: Alexander the Great
lessons.text1: Alexander the Great was the king of Macedonia in 336 BCE. His goal was to claim more power. He became an impressive leader and managed to create an empire across three continents by his death at just 32 years old.

lessons.name: Alexander Hamilton
lessons.text1: Alexander Hamilton caught the attention of George Washington and became Washington's aide. Hamilton trained as a lawyer and joined the Constitutional Convention to represent New York. He is considered one of the founding fathers of the U.S. Constitution.

lessons.name: Ada Lovelace
lessons.text1: Ada Lovelace worked with an inventor who designed a machine called the "Analytical Engine," a precursor to the modern computer. Lovelace wrote the first algorithm that was intended to be processed by a machine, making her the first computer programmer.

lessons.name: Rosa Parks
lessons.text1: Rosa Parks was an American civil rights activist. She was arrested for sitting in the whites-only section of a bus in Alabama in 1955, refusing to give up her seat and move to the back of the bus. Her actions inspired other boycotts and non-violent protests against segregation.

lessons.name: Julius Caesar
lessons.text1: Julius Caesar was a ruler known for leading his troops and claiming a vast amount of power for the Roman republic in 44 BCE. He was assassinated by a group of his own republican senators because they thought he wanted to bring back the monarchy, a form of government with just one ruler.

lessons.name: Anne Frank
lessons.text1: During World War II, Anne Frank, a German-born Jewish girl, hid from the Nazis in an attic in Amsterdam alongside her family. During this time, Anne wrote a diary that captured her thoughts and feelings. This diary was later published and became one of the most famous and best-selling books in the world.

lessons.name: Architectural Wonders Introduction
lessons.text1: Our world has amazing structures built with creativity and hard work. Practice your typing skills while learning about incredible architectural wonders.

lessons.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
lessons.text1: The Great Pyramid of Giza in Cairo, Egypt was built in the early 26th century BCE and stands at about 450 feet tall.

lessons.name: Tokyo Sky Tree
lessons.text1: At 2,080 feet tall, the Tokyo Sky Tree is the second-tallest structure in the world, surpassed only by the Burj Khalifa building in Dubai.

lessons.name: Sydney Opera House
lessons.text1: Danish architect Jørn Utzon sketched the Sydney Opera House in Australia as part of a competition. His iconic design was originally rejected three times before it won.

lessons.name: Colosseum
lessons.text1: The Colosseum in Rome, Italy is the largest amphitheater of Roman architecture. It stands 164 feet tall and was the model for many other construction projects after its completion.

lessons.name: Alhambra
lessons.text1: Perched on a hill above Granada, Spain, the Alhambra is an iconic landmark. This castle-like structure was the palace fortress for Moorish and Spanish rulers. It now gets over 5,000 visitors per day.

lessons.name: Zapotec
lessons.text1: The archaeological site Monte Alban towers above the Oaxaca valleys and symbolizes the power of its builders, the Zapotec people. Built around 500 CE, today it serves as an abandoned site for tourists to visit.

lessons.name: Meenakshi-Sundareswarar
lessons.text1: The Chola temples are everywhere in Tamil Nadu, India, but one stands out for its height and beauty. The Meenakshi-Sundareswarar Temple is over 150 feet tall and decorated with colorful deities, demons, warriors, maidens, and sprites.

lessons.name: Peyrepertuse
lessons.text1: Seeing the French castle Peyrepertuse for the first time is unforgettable. Built 800 years ago, it resembles a rock formation atop a mountain, but it's a genuine castle! Workers hauled stones to create one of Europe's most majestic structures.

lessons.name: Architectural Wonders Game 1
lessons.text1: pyramid Tokyo structure building architect amphitheater landmark archaeological temples castle

lessons.name: Great Mosque
lessons.text1: The Great Mosque in Cordoba, Spain was built in the 8th century. It was the second largest mosque in the world. In 1236, it was converted into a cathedral. Its beautiful interior and colorful arches attract visitors from all over.

lessons.name: Bayterek Tower
lessons.text1: One of Kazakhstan's coolest buildings is the Bayterek Tower. This tall, spiky building resembles a tree with a giant orb in its branches. It symbolizes a legend in which a magical bird laid its golden egg in a tall poplar tree.

lessons.name: Wat Phra Kaew
lessons.text1: Wat Phra Kaew in Thailand is a stunning temple located at the Grand Palace. Its shiny walls and colorful decorations make it sparkle. Many people visit to see the tiny Emerald Buddha, the most important statue in the country.

lessons.name: Taj Mahal
lessons.text1: The Taj Mahal in Agra, India is the most famous tomb in the world. It was built in 1653 by Emperor Shah Jahan for his wife. Made of beautiful marble, its colors seem to change throughout the day from pink in the morning to gold at night.

lessons.name: Largest Swimming Pool
lessons.text1: How big do you think the largest swimming pool in the world is? As of 2023, the largest one is the Citystars Sharm El Sheikh in Egypt, and it's over a million square feet! This one, like many other swimming pools around the world, is actually a man-made lagoon!

lessons.name: Guggenheim Museum
lessons.text1: The Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain has several connected buildings made of a shiny, wavy metal. It was designed by the famous architect Frank Gehry and opened in 1997. The museum attracts millions of visitors who come to see its amazing shapes and modern art inside.

lessons.name: Angkor Wat
lessons.text1: Angkor Wat in Cambodia was built over 800 years ago by King Suryavarman II. It is the largest religious temple in the world. Originally a Hindu temple, it became a Buddhist temple in the 13th century CE and is still used today. This structure even appears on the Cambodian flag!

lessons.name: Beijing's National Stadium
lessons.text1: Beijing's National Stadium, known as the Bird's Nest, is the largest steel structure in the world! Inside, there is a huge space where the 2008 Summer Olympics opening and closing ceremonies took place. Many people visit the Bird's Nest to admire its amazing design and impressive size.

lessons.name: Petronas Towers
lessons.text1: The Petronas Towers in Malaysia have 88 floors and are shaped like an "M." Standing 452 meters tall, they are connected by the world's highest double-decker bridge between the 41st and 42nd floors. People can walk on the bridge for amazing views, and it helps keep the towers strong during powerful winds.

lessons.name: Folklore and Mythology Introduction
lessons.text1: Myths and folklore are two of the oldest types of stories. Let's learn some interesting facts about them while practicing our typing!

lessons.name: Creation Myths
lessons.text1: Myths are the sacred stories of a culture. Creation myths say what happened "in the beginning" and explain natural phenomena. Almost every culture has one!

lessons.name: Pangu
lessons.text1: In a Chinese creation myth, the giant Pangu hatched from an egg. His eyes became the sun and moon. His body became the landscape. His lice eventually became humanity!

lessons.name: Zodiac
lessons.text1: The zodiac is an astrological system based on mythology. Many people know the Greek, Chinese, and Vedic zodiacs, but there are many others, including the Celtic, Babylonian, Maya, and Egyptian.

lessons.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
lessons.text1: One of the oldest surviving written myths is The Epic of Gilgamesh. It was written almost 4,000 years ago. The code to reading the ancient script was cracked in the 1870s, bringing the story back to life!

lessons.name: Egyptian Gods
lessons.text1: Many ancient Egyptian gods were depicted as having animal heads and human bodies. For example, Anubis, the god of embalming, had the head of a jackal. Sekhmet, the goddess of war, had the head of a lioness.

lessons.name: Dragons
lessons.text1: Dragons appear in ancient mythology all over the world, despite limited communication between those early societies. European dragons were often depicted as fearsome treasure-hoarders, while Chinese dragons were depicted as wise, lucky, and bringers of prosperity.

lessons.name: Days of the Week
lessons.text1: Most of our days of the week get their names from Norse mythology. Sunday and Monday come from Sol and Mani, the Sun and Moon. Tuesday is Tyr's Day, Wednesday is Woden's Day, Thursday is Thor's Day, and Friday is Frigg's Day. Saturday is the odd one out; it's named for Saturn, an ancient Roman god.

lessons.name: Dreamtime
lessons.text1: Australian Aboriginal cultures are some of the oldest in the world, dating back more than 60,000 years. Their mythologies are among the oldest, too! In Aboriginal religion, spirits created the world in Dreamtime. Dreamtime is both a time and a place, encompassing the past, the present, and the future.

lessons.text1: dragons mythology Norse Australian Aboriginal creation nature Pangu Gilgamesh zodiac Anubis Thor Dreamtime

lessons.name: Folklore
lessons.text1: Folklore and myths are similar. But while myths often focus on universal truths, folklore focuses on people, animals, and everyday events. And while myths are often set in the ancient past, folklore may have more to do with recent history or local legends. Most places have interesting folktales of their own!

lessons.name: Lost Dutchman's Mine
lessons.text1: The Lost Dutchman's Mine is a legendary gold mine somewhere in Arizona's Superstition Mountains. "The Dutchman" himself, Jacob Waltz, was said to have found the mine in the 1870s. Before he died, he supposedly described the location of the mine to his neighbor, but no one has ever been able to find it.

lessons.name: Knock on Wood
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen someone knock on wood to ward off bad luck? No one knows for certain where this superstition came from. One theory links it to the ancient Celtic practice of knocking on trees to ask spirits for protection. Another links it to a 19th-century children's game called Tiggy Touchwood.

lessons.name: Bigfoot
lessons.text1: Since 1969, it has been illegal to hunt and kill Bigfoot in Skamania County, Washington. This law was likely put in place by lawmakers to prevent armed Bigfoot hunters from entering Skamania en masse. Luckily, scientists and tourists are still welcome to come and peacefully investigate any Bigfoot sightings!

lessons.name: Icelandic Sagas
lessons.text1: Iceland was settled by the Vikings in the 9th and 10th centuries. The Vikings detailed this settlement in medieval history books known as the Icelandic sagas. The sagas blended folklore and fact, documenting historical events while weaving in supernatural elements like prophecies, monsters, and ghosts!

lessons.name: The Pied Piper
lessons.text1: The Pied Piper is a folkloric figure who played his flute to lead rats out of the town of Hamelin. When the townspeople refused to pay him, he played his flute to lead their children away, and they disappeared. While this is only a story, historical records suggest that it may have been based on a true incident.

lessons.name: Robin Hood
lessons.text1: Robin Hood is the heroic outlaw of legend who steals from the rich and gives to the poor. He probably never existed, but parts of the story are based in reality. Robin Hood and his merry band of thieves lived in Sherwood Forest, a real location in England. You can even visit the famous oak tree they used as their hideout!

lessons.name: Vanishing Hitchhiker
lessons.text1: Have you ever heard of the vanishing hitchhiker? Late at night, a driver spots a hitchhiker on the side of the road. The hitchhiker gets into the car and the driver continues on their way, only to be shocked to find the hitchhiker has vanished! This spooky story is told all over the world, with lots of local variations.

lessons.name: Cow Tipping
lessons.text1: You've probably heard of cow tipping, a prank in which a group of people sneak up on a sleeping cow and tip it onto its side. But did you know cow tipping doesn't really exist? Cows don't sleep standing up, and they rarely let strangers approach them at night, and if they were somehow tipped, they could easily stand back up!
